newsitem.title: TURKEY: President keeps Turks guessing on new PM.
newsitem.headline: President keeps Turks guessing on new PM.

text.p: President Suleyman Demirel is keeping Turkey guessing on his choice of a prime minister to succeed Islamist Necmettin Erbakan, who was forced out this week by army pressure.
Demirel's talks with opposition party leaders have failed to yield an immediate decision and his office did not list any further meeting with political leaders on his Friday diary.
Mesut Yilmaz of the conservative Motherland Party, one of the main contenders, met Demirel for an hour on Thursday and told reporters:
"I told him I was ready to take on the responsibility."
The opposition leader has 129 MPs in the 550-seat assembly and could struggle to find coalition allies if named as prime minister designate to succeed Erbakan who resigned on Wednesday.
Shares in Istanbul leapt over two percent on hopes Erbakan's resignation would end months of political turmoil that have dogged markets and upset government plans for a balanced budget.
Tansu Ciller, Yilmaz's conservative rival, has also been tipped as being in line to get the government mandate after a stormy year in coalition with Erbakan's Islamist Welfare Party .
Erbakan stepped down after persistent accusations that he was trying to slowly dissolve NATO member Turkey's official secularist system and create an Islamic state similar to Iran.
Ciller said her opponents in the scramble for the top job did not have the support to win a confidence vote in parliament.
"They have not established a majority and it is not clear who would be their prime minister," she told a news conference.
Pro-Western Ciller has the backing of Erbakan's Islamists for a plan to head a caretaker administration and take Turkey to early polls.

A revamped alliance headed by Ciller would command the support on paper of 282 MPs in the 550-member assembly but some of her True Path Party have threatened to abandon her if she does not make a complete break with Erbakan.
The Islamist-led coalition collapsed under a secularist onslaught launched by the generals in February.
The army ousted three governments between 1960-80 and has a large say in daily life in much of the Southeast where emergency rule has been imposed as part of the fight against Kurdish rebels.

Turkish forces have begun a partial withdrawal from northern Iraq after a five-week operation against Kurdistan Workers Party rebels who stage attacks into Turkey from the mountains there, Anatolian news agency said on Thursday.
But the generals promised to press on with the domestic campaign against rising Islamic radicalism despite Erbakan's resignation.
"The mission of the Turkish armed forces of protecting the Turkish republic's unity against the threat of fundamentalism is still valid and continuing," a senior military official told Reuters.
